doc.title: Joseph Rene and Edna Kelly Interview, 1969-12-15

title: Economy Hall dances, his song, and a white cornetist; Chris's start on tin
summary: Edna describes the hall and Chris's composed song for her, a white cornetist who played Chris's tunes, and how Chris began on a tin horn in the country.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band

blocks.x: Well, now, describe to me what it was like when you say you would get to economy hall and the dance would begin. What would it be like? Oh, beautiful.

The hall would be all lit up and the stand would be up like a grandstand, you know. The musicians would be up and the floor would be waxed. And the girls, the society girls, you know, would take the paper, you know, decorate it. It was beautiful. And have a police at the door at that time. What about the music? What can you tell me about the music? Oh, they play music. They get up there and play so easy to tell his love. Now, he'd composed that song. But he waited too long to, you know, to take it up. And he didn't take it up. You know what that song name? That's Kelly's love. He composed that song. That's his song. He composed that song to me. And after he didn't do anything with the song, they took the song, whoever took it, and they put a chalice, chalice love. Yeah.
Well, how did he play? Can you describe the way he followed the song? Yeah, he could play some music.

He could play some good cornet. You know that, he from the French Quarter. He's a white man. He's kind of a cell man. He's got a little ball right up here, and he plays a cornet. He's a cell man. A white man? A white man, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And he's kind of ball-headed. He plays in the band. I heard him play. Played in what band? I don't know, but I know he can play some cornet. And that man played in the tune of my husband. Oh, really? He's white. And he's a subtle man. Wouldn't think he knows how to play. And he really can play. A subtle man?
He's not no young man at all. Oh, I see.

That's not John Lee Wiggs. It must be. It might be. John Lee Wiggs. Somebody say something like John. He'd be with a fellow that called Chris. A white fellow that called Chris from the French Quarter. Do you know him? They got band music. They go through. You know, um... Sheik. Yeah.
I know Sheik. Well, Sheik. She knows them all. Sheik knows them. Yeah.
I know. I know. I know.
And then Sheik used to play with my husband. Yes. That's right.
She used to take lessons for him. That's right.
Did anybody else take lessons for him?
Yeah. He did. Let's see. What's his name?

About stuff Only that. He said when he first started he was living in the country. A place by the name of St. Sophie. That's the name of the place. And he said he was sitting on a levee. You know what you call a levee, huh? By the river. And he got a piece of tin and bent it and tried to blow like and put holes in it. And he got music out of it. And by-by, he kept on, kept on. And he brought him a little brass horn. And he started playing in little concerts, you used to call them at that time. You know, concerts. And the people used to dance up to music. So by-by, when he got up a little high, well he brought him up over. But he was a good one.
